newsitem.title: USA: Illinois judge won't suppress tobacco papers.
newsitem.headline: Illinois judge won't suppress tobacco papers.

text.p: An Illinois circuit court judge Monday denied a request from tobacco industry lawyers to prevent release of sensitive internal documents by Liggett Group, an attorney for the Illinois Attorney General's office said.

"This is a distinct victory for the people of Illinois, who have a right to prosecute their case against tobacco," David Kistenbroker of the state attorney general's office, said after the ruling by Cook County Circuit Court Judge Richard Neville.

Neville ordered Liggett to deliver to him by Friday, under seal, certain documents the cigarette maker agreed last week to release in an historic settlement between it and 22 state attorneys general, Kistenbroker said.
He said Neville will review the documents and decide within 30 days what to do with them.
Liggett asserted in court that it would comply with the judge's order, Kistenbroker said.

Liggett Group, the smallest U.S. tobacco company and a unit of Brooke Group Ltd, agreed last Thursday to settle tobacco litigation with attorneys general from 22 states and give up potentially damaging documents.

The attorneys general are suing the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid health costs of poor smokers. While the settlement removes Liggett as a defendant in the lawsuits, the accord will not protect the company, owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd., from any criminal action.

As part of the unprecedented deal, Liggett not only became the first tobacco company to admit that smoking is addictive, but also agreed to turn over documents that could shed light on the knowledge and beliefs of executives at other tobacco companies about the health risks of smoking and whether they purposely marketed cigarettes to youth.

The tobacco companies quickly obtained a restraining order from a North Carolina state court barring Liggett from giving up documents protected by attorney-client privilege. However, attorneys general said that if it is found the papers show criminal activity, they would not be protected.
